voice.refText: You wake up and discover you can pause time. 10 seconds once a day. At first, you use it for dumb things. You catch your falling coffee. You dodge your boss in the hallway.

Friend.describe: A warm, relaxed male baritone: a man of about thirty who runs a food stall with his best friend. Quick, joking, laughs before his own punchline, a light Singapore English lilt. Close and easy, never loud.

Worker.describe: A cheerful, gravelly male bass: a city maintenance worker in his fifties up a ladder. Gruff, satisfied, talking to himself.

Coffee seller.describe: A dry, brisk female alto: a woman in her fifties who runs the coffee stall next door. Low and a little husky, unimpressed, few words, a faint Singapore English lilt.

Kid.describe: A high, bright boy's voice, about ten years old. Quick, cheeky, outraged when he loses.

Magician.describe: A bright, theatrical male baritone: a street magician in his forties. Showy and warm, a performer's lift on every word.

Date.describe: A flat, bored female mezzo: a woman of about thirty on a dull dinner date. Dry, deadpan, eyes on her phone.

Pickpocket.describe: A hoarse, nervous male baritone: a thin man in his thirties. Quick, defensive, a little breathless.

Landlord.describe: A smooth, cool male baritone: a landlord in his sixties. Polite, unhurried, quietly cold, every word measured.

Coach.describe: A loud, upbeat male baritone: a street salesman in his forties. Bouncy and confident, a pitch voice, every line a slogan.

Sister.describe: A small, frightened female mezzo: a young woman in her twenties on a phone line. Hushed and quick, trying to stay calm.

lines.text: Closing time. A food court in Singapore.

lines.text: So what if an AI predicted every choice you make, and paid you every time it was right?
lines.say: [curious, leaning in on the question, a small smile on the last clause] So what if an AI predicted every choice you make, and paid you every time it was right?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Every night you count the box. Every night he holds out his hand. Every night you pocket the key. The oldest joke you two have. Tonight it came with a number.
lines.say: [warm, fond, a rhythm like a habit, then the last sentence dropped quiet] Every night you count the box. Every night he holds out his hand. Every night you pocket the key. The oldest joke you two have. Tonight it came with a number.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Do what the tag says, and your rent halves. Don't, and every head in the court turns. And here's the thing. It's right ninety-nine times in a hundred. About everybody.
lines.say: [brisk, a dealer laying out terms, a shade colder on the turning heads, the last two words hushed as a hook] Do what the tag says, and your rent halves. Don't, and every head in the court turns. And here's the thing. It's right ninety-nine times in a hundred. About everybody.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Over every head, a tag. What you'll do in the next ten seconds, and how sure the city is. It watches from every lamppost.
lines.say: [clear, exact, the rule said once, a glance upward on the last line] Over every head, a tag. What you'll do in the next ten seconds, and how sure the city is. It watches from every lamppost.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Do what it says, and everything gets cheaper. Your coffee. Your fare. Your rent. It knows you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, it knows you.
lines.say: [plain, each item a small gift, then slower and almost tender on the last sentence] Do what it says, and everything gets cheaper. Your coffee. Your fare. Your rent. It knows you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, it knows you.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Break it, and your tag goes crimson where everyone can see, and your prices climb. One more thing. It knows every choice you've ever made. It has never seen one you haven't. Remember that.
lines.say: [measured, a warning without heat, each limit its own beat, the last two words almost a whisper] Break it, and your tag goes crimson where everyone can see, and your prices climb. One more thing. It knows every choice you've ever made. It has never seen one you haven't. Remember that.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: He hums all the way home. He stops. It saw that too.
lines.say: [amused, fond, the last sentence dry] He hums all the way home. He stops. It saw that too.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: It likes me.
lines.say: [delighted, walking backwards, arms out, loud] It likes me.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Nobody here finds a price on a choice strange. This city has billed drivers for its busiest roads by time of day since 1998.
lines.say: [dry, matter of fact, a shrug in the voice] Nobody here finds a price on a choice strange. This city has billed drivers for its busiest roads by time of day since nineteen ninety-eight.

lines.text: Tomorrow you'll find out which way yours moves.

lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Morning. You've worked it out. It guesses. So guess wrong.
lines.say: [brisk, confident, a little mischievous, a dare on the last three words] Morning. You've worked it out. It guesses. So guess wrong.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Four reds. Up twenty-five before breakfast.
lines.say: [deadpan, the joke landing dry, a wince on the number] Four reds. Up twenty-five before breakfast.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A professor once wrote a tiny program that guessed which of two keys people would press when they tried to type at random. Right seventy to eighty per cent of the time. He couldn't beat it himself.
lines.say: [calm, a story told at a table, a small amused weight on the last sentence] A professor once wrote a tiny program that guessed which of two keys people would press when they tried to type at random. Right seventy to eighty per cent of the time. He couldn't beat it himself.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Trying to be random is a pattern.
lines.say: [flat, the landing line, a complete thought] Trying to be random is a pattern.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So your coffee this morning costs more than it did last night.
lines.say: [dry, sympathetic, landing on you] So your coffee this morning costs more than it did last night.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Coffee seller: You're up today.
lines.say: [dry, eyebrows up, tapping the board, not unkind] You're up today.

lines.text: Your best friend tries a coin.

lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Problem one. Being random costs money. But the city worked that out long ago. And it's playing a different game.
lines.say: [leaning in, a storyteller numbering the trouble, the last sentence low and a little ominous] Problem one: being random costs money. But the city worked that out long ago. And it's playing a different game.

lines.text: The platform. The kid with the cap plays rock-paper-scissors with the man beside him. Wins with rock. His tag says rock again. Eighty-three.
lines.say: [amused, quick, a commentator at a small match, the number dropped like a punchline] The platform. The kid with the cap plays rock-paper-scissors with the man beside him. Wins with rock. His tag says rock again. Eighty-three.

lines.text: The magician.

lines.text: His tag says which card. By lunch, no act.

lines.text: A couple on a date. Her tag: checks phone. His: same joke. Both obey. Half price.

lines.text: Date: Heard this one.

lines.text: Then the first crimson the city has seen.

lines.text: Every head turns. Doors shut on him. The coffee seller won't pour. A crimson tag is a verdict everyone can read, and nobody asks for the trial. By the weekend his tag says stands still. Safest man on the platform.
lines.say: [cold and quick on the first three sentences, then slow and level on the verdict, then dry and a little sorry on the ending] Every head turns. Doors shut on him. The coffee seller won't pour. A crimson tag is a verdict everyone can read, and nobody asks for the trial. By the weekend his tag says stands still. Safest man on the platform.

lines.text: Phone records from fifty thousand people once showed where a person will be is, in principle, guessable up to about ninety-three per cent of the time. Nobody fell below eighty per cent.

lines.text: You thought you were a free spirit. You're a timetable.

lines.text: The landlord's letter.

lines.text: People farm it. In 1902, Hanoi paid a bounty for every rat tail, and officials found people breeding rats for the tails. Pay for predictability, and people breed it.
lines.say: [amused, a story with a sting, the last sentence slow and exact] People farm it. In nineteen oh two, Hanoi paid a bounty for every rat tail, and officials found people breeding rats for the tails. Pay for predictability, and people breed it.

lines.say: [a street seller's chant, upbeat, selling it] Same route. Same lunch. Same face.

lines.say: [quick and wry on the magician, then slower, the numbers dropping like coins, the last sentence quiet and a little uneasy] The magician reads tags for tips. Your rate falls. Sixty-one. Fifty-five. You've learned to read your tag before you reach.

lines.text: His phone lights up on the counter. His sister. He turns it face down. You don't ask.

lines.say: [very quiet, slow, hurt held in, no music under it] He reads the sixty-two. He shuts his mouth. He counts coins instead.

lines.text: That's what the discount costs. Not money.
lines.say: [low, level, the point landing] That's what the discount costs. Not money.

lines.text: You count the box. That's the habit.
lines.say: [flat, tired, close] You count the box. That's the habit.

lines.text: And the board says ninety-nine point five now. It's getting better. Or something is.
lines.say: [quiet, a hook, the last three words slower and colder] And the board says ninety-nine point five now. It's getting better. Or something is.

lines.text: You thought it read minds. Nothing reads minds.
lines.say: [plain, a correction said gently] You thought it read minds. Nothing reads minds.

lines.text: In 2008, brain scans could guess whether a person would press a left or a right button a few seconds before they felt they'd chosen. The guess was right about sixty times in a hundred. A coin gets fifty.
lines.say: [clear, careful, a story told exactly, the last sentence dry] In two thousand and eight, brain scans could guess whether a person would press a left or a right button a few seconds before they felt they'd chosen. The guess was right about sixty times in a hundred. A coin gets fifty.

lines.text: Sixty. And the card over you says ninety-nine. So where's the other thirty-nine coming from?
lines.say: [slow, puzzled, the question held open, not answered] Sixty. And the card over you says ninety-nine. So where's the other thirty-nine coming from?

lines.text: Quiet all week. Then tonight, the landlord impression. The napkin tie. The one that always gets you.
lines.say: [warm, relieved, a laugh under it, fond on the last sentence] Quiet all week. Then tonight, the landlord impression. The napkin tie. The one that always gets you.

lines.text: Friend: It knows the bit.
lines.say: [quiet, the smile gone, pulling the napkin off] It knows the bit.

lines.text: At six in the morning his tag says counts coins. At ten at night, checks phone.
lines.say: [hushed, worried, each time of day its own picture] At six in the morning his tag says counts coins. At ten at night, checks phone.

lines.text: Tomorrow his hand comes out, like every night. And the tag over it won't be a joke.
lines.say: [low, a dread building under a plain voice, the last five words slow] Tomorrow his hand comes out, like every night. And the tag over it won't be a joke.

lines.text: Closing. The court half dark. His hand comes out.
lines.say: [hushed, short, the breath held] Closing. The court half dark. His hand comes out.

lines.text: Friend: Trust me?
lines.say: Trust me?

lines.say: [a laugh that starts and stops halfway, shaken] Machine's drunk.

lines.text: He laughs. It stops halfway.
lines.say: [very quiet, flat] He laughs. It stops halfway.

lines.text: You've put that key in your pocket a thousand times. Tonight it's the first time you've locked something away from him.
lines.say: [low, slow, tender and hurt, the landing line finished] You've put that key in your pocket a thousand times. Tonight it's the first time you've locked something away from him.

lines.text: Coffee seller: Not with that tag.
lines.say: [firm, not cruel, eyes on the card not the man] Not with that tag.

lines.text: Landlord: Nothing personal.
lines.say: [clipped, eyes down, an envelope held out] Nothing personal.
lines.speaker: Landlord

lines.text: His rent doubles. His coffee's gone. He's the pickpocket now. To everyone but you.
lines.say: [flat, each blow short, the last four words warmer] His rent doubles. His coffee's gone. He's the pickpocket now. To everyone but you.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But the tag doesn't say thief. It says seventy-one. And you're about to learn who gets a seventy-one.
lines.say: [leaning in, low, a hook, the number said twice with weight] But the tag doesn't say thief. It says seventy-one. And you're about to learn who gets a seventy-one.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: In America, a risk score used in courts wrongly flagged Black defendants as future criminals at almost twice the rate of white defendants.
lines.say: [level, serious, exact, no heat] In America, a risk score used in courts wrongly flagged Black defendants as future criminals at almost twice the rate of white defendants.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And a crowd of strangers online, given two lines about each defendant, predicted who'd reoffend about as well as the software did.
lines.say: [calm, a shade of disbelief, slower on the last clause] And a crowd of strangers online, given two lines about each defendant, predicted who'd reoffend about as well as the software did.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It isn't seeing a thief. It's seeing a man in trouble. And it can't tell the two apart. Neither can the food court.
lines.say: [quiet, sad, the landing line complete, the last sentence a little bitter] It isn't seeing a thief. It's seeing a man in trouble. And it can't tell the two apart. Neither can the food court.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Every night his number climbs. Seventy-one. Eighty. Eighty-eight. Fewer people sit near the stall. You count the box alone.
lines.say: [slow, the numbers like footsteps, the last sentence quiet and lonely] Every night his number climbs. Seventy-one. Eighty. Eighty-eight. Fewer people sit near the stall. You count the box alone.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Sister: Are they gone yet?
lines.say: [small, tinny, frightened, down a phone line] Are they gone yet?

lines.text: Friend: My sister's fine.
lines.say: [too quick, too bright, a smile forced on] My sister's fine.

lines.text: You both read it.
lines.say: [flat, very quiet] You both read it.

lines.text: The month ends. Rent's due tomorrow. Both your rents, in one tin box.
lines.say: [low, steady, the stakes counted, the last phrase slow] The month ends. Rent's due tomorrow. Both your rents, in one tin box.

lines.text: And that's when his tag says the thing the whole court has been waiting for.
lines.say: [hushed, a held breath, a hook] And that's when his tag says the thing the whole court has been waiting for.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Closing. The last customers gone. The coffee seller's phone is already up. Because his tag says takes the box. Ninety-four.
lines.say: [quiet, tight, each sentence shorter, the number alone and cold] Closing. The last customers gone. The coffee seller's phone is already up. Because his tag says takes the box. Ninety-four.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Everything it ever got right about you was a coffee, a train, a key. When scientists watched people choose where real charity money would go, the famous early brain signal was missing.
lines.say: [low, thinking aloud, then careful and exact on the fact] Everything it ever got right about you was a coffee, a train, a key. When scientists watched people choose where real charity money would go, the famous early brain signal was missing.

lines.text: It has never seen you choose something that mattered. And you're about to.
lines.say: [slow, intimate, the last four words almost a dare] It has never seen you choose something that mattered. And you're about to.

lines.text: A month of half price. What did you stop doing for it?
lines.say: [quiet, a question to you and nobody else, no answer offered] A month of half price. What did you stop doing for it?

lines.text: Pocket the key, and the city's right, and your rent stays half. Hold it out, and your tag goes crimson in front of everyone. And so, maybe, does your money.
lines.say: [level, two doors held open, no lean either way, the last clause slower] Pocket the key, and the city's right, and your rent stays half. Hold it out, and your tag goes crimson in front of everyone. And so, maybe, does your money.

lines.text: You take the key out of your pocket.

lines.text: Ninety-four.
lines.say: [one word, very quiet, then nothing] Ninety-four.

lines.text: The first blank card the city has ever made.
lines.say: [hushed, awed, slow] The first blank card the city has ever made.

lines.say: [broken, barely out, eyes on the key] I was going to.

lines.text: You can't steal what you've just been handed. And the machine had no card for that.
lines.say: [quiet, warm, certain, the landing line complete] You can't steal what you've just been handed. And the machine had no card for that.

lines.text: Two crimson cards. Every face in the court turns toward them. Nothing else moves.

lines.text: It knows you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, it knows you. No. You knew it. And did what it said.
lines.say: [the planted line said back soft, then a hard stop on the No, then slow and clear] It knows you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, it knows you. No. You knew it. And did what it said.

lines.text: Drivers tracked by their insurer for a discount braked hard about a fifth less often within six months. The watching changed the driving.

lines.text: An economist put it in 1975: lean on a number to control people, and the number stops behaving.
lines.say: [dry, a rule from an old book, the last four words slow] An economist put it in nineteen seventy-five: lean on a number to control people, and the number stops behaving.

lines.text: Run the board backwards. Ninety-nine. Ninety-three. Eighty-four. Seventy-one. The night it started, it was right seven times in ten.
lines.say: [quiet, the numbers falling like a countdown, the last sentence flat and surprised] Run the board backwards. Ninety-nine. Ninety-three. Eighty-four. Seventy-one. The night it started, it was right seven times in ten.

lines.text: A hundred and sixty teams once got thousands of facts about thousands of families, to predict how the children's lives would turn out. The best predictions were only slightly better than a simple guess from four facts.
lines.say: [calm, a story told exactly, a shade of wonder on the last clause] A hundred and sixty teams once got thousands of facts about thousands of families, to predict how the children's lives would turn out. The best predictions were only slightly better than a simple guess from four facts.

lines.text: Machines are bad at people. Until people get simple.
